title: Gauge for amigurumi
subtitle: Why amigurumi needs tight tension and a smaller hook than the yarn label suggests
excerpt: Amigurumi gauge is different from garment gauge. For a stuffed toy, the goal is a fabric dense enough that the stuffing inside does not show through between stitches. This means using a hook one to two sizes smaller than the yarn label recommends and working at a tighter tension than usual.
sourceNotes: Edie Eckman, The Crochet Answer Book (Storey Publishing). Contemporary amigurumi design references.

glossaryTerms.definition: The tight, dense tension used for stuffed crochet figures, produced by working with a hook one to two sizes smaller than the yarn label recommends. The closed fabric prevents stuffing from showing through the stitches.
When white or light-coloured fibrefill stuffing is visible through gaps in the crochet fabric, particularly in darker coloured pieces worked at too loose a tension.

content.text: is tighter than the tension you would use for the same yarn in a garment or blanket. A stuffed toy needs the stitches to sit close enough together that the fibrefill inside does not show through as
. The way to achieve this is to use a crochet hook one to two sizes smaller than the yarn ball band recommends.

A DK-weight yarn normally works at a 4.0 mm hook. For amigurumi in the same DK yarn, use a 3.0 mm or 3.5 mm hook. The fabric will feel stiffer and less drapey than DK worked at the label hook size. This stiffness is what you want; it gives the finished toy its firm, rounded shape.

items.name: DK or aran weight yarn
items.note: Smooth yarn shows the stitch structure more clearly. Avoid very fluffy or loopy yarns for amigurumi, as they hide the stitch tops and make counting difficult.

items.name: Crochet hook, one to two sizes smaller than the label recommends
items.note: For DK yarn: 3.0 mm or 3.5 mm. For aran yarn: 4.0 mm or 4.5 mm.

items.name: Measuring tape
items.note: For checking the piece dimensions against the pattern as it grows.

items.name: Stitch markers
items.note: Essential for tracking the beginning of rounds in spiral amigurumi construction.

content.text: Amigurumi patterns give a tension in stitches and rows per 10 cm, or as a finished diameter for a specific number of increase rounds. Check your tension against the pattern's stated measurement:
Work the magic ring and the first three increase rounds (the standard start for a sphere): magic ring, 6 dc (UK) into ring; increase to 12; increase to 18. Measure the diameter of the resulting disc.
If the pattern says this should be 4.5 cm across and your disc measures 5.5 cm, go down one more hook size.
Hold the work up to a light source and look through the fabric. The stitches should be close enough together that you cannot see daylight clearly through them.
Why amigurumi tension matters more than garment tension

A garment worked at the wrong tension comes out the wrong size; it still works as a garment. An amigurumi worked at a loose tension looks hollow or lumpy because the white stuffing shows through the dark outer fabric, and the piece does not hold a firm, rounded shape when stuffed.

Working at a tighter tension for long sessions can cause hand or wrist fatigue more quickly than loose-tension work. If you feel discomfort, stop and rest rather than continuing. For amigurumi with many small pieces, break the work into shorter sessions or switch between tight amigurumi work and a looser-tension project to rest the hands.

items.symptom: White stuffing shows through dark-coloured fabric
items.cause: The hook size is too large for the yarn weight, producing gaps between stitches.
items.fix: Unravel and rework at a smaller hook size. Test the new gauge by holding the worked fabric up to a light. If you can see through it clearly, go down another hook size.

items.symptom: The hook is very difficult to insert into the stitches
items.cause: The tension is too tight: the hook is smaller than necessary, or the working tension is being applied too firmly.
items.fix: Move up half a hook size or consciously relax the grip on the working yarn. Amigurumi fabric should be dense, not locked solid.

items.symptom: The finished piece is the right tension but the wrong finished size
items.cause: Tension gauge matches but the pattern called for a different yarn weight than was used.
items.fix: The finished size of an amigurumi is directly related to the yarn weight. Thicker yarn at the same tension produces a larger toy; finer yarn produces a smaller one. Adjust the yarn weight rather than the tension if a specific size is required.

content.text: A simple sphere is the best first amigurumi tension test: it uses only increase rounds, straight rounds, and decrease rounds. Work one sphere at the yarn label's recommended hook size and one at a hook two sizes smaller. Stuff both and compare the result. The tighter-tension sphere will be smaller, firmer, and less transparent.
